text:
A: Hiya, er, can you hear us alright?
B: Yeah, hiya. Can you hear me?
A: Aye, loud and clear. I'm Craig.
B: Oh. That's my husband's name. *(laughs)* Sorry, that threw me a bit. I'm Gemma.
A: Ha, good name, that. Where are you, then?
B: Bloxwich. It's Walsall, sort of. West Midlands.
A: Right, aye. I'm Hartlepool, up the North East, on the coast.
B: Is that near Newcastle?
A: Bit further down, like, between Sunderland and Middlesbrough. Everyone says Newcastle, it's fine. Yeah... er. Was that puzzle alright for you? I sort of lost the plot halfway through.
B: Erm, no, I was rubbish at the shapes one. I just clicked something in the end.
A: Same. I thought it was just me, honestly.
B: No, definitely not just you.
A: What do you do yourself, Gemma?
B: I just run a shift really. At a parcel depot off the M6, by Cannock. Late shift.
A: How many on a shift, like?
B: About forty. And two team leaders.
A: Forty! That's not "just" anything, that. That's a lot of folk to keep happy.
B: *(laughs)* Erm, I don't know. Most of them are alright, to be fair. It's the run-up to Christmas you dread, it's rammed, parcels everywhere. Sorry, what do you do?
A: Er, I'm a brickie. Well, I was. I've been off with me back about a year and a half now, so I'm sort of in between things, you know.
B: Oh, that's rubbish. Sorry.
A: Nah, it's alright, it's just one of them things. The physio says walk, so I walk the seafront. The wind coming in off the sea, though, it'd take your face off.
B: My Craig's a plasterer. Self-employed. He's always going on about his back as well.
A: Aye, tell him to look after it, 'cause I didn't. You think you're fine till you're not, like. You're lifting blocks all day and you don't think twice. Then one morning I bent down to tie me boot and that was it, couldn't get back up. Me mam had to ring the doctor for us. Thirty-three and me mam's ringing the doctor.
B: Oh no. That must've been horrible.
A: Aye, it was a bit daft really. Anyway. Does he leave dust everywhere? Plasterers are the worst for it. We used to say you could follow 'em round site by the footprints.
B: *(laughs)* Yeah, it's all over the van. And the hall. I've given up. Dolly comes in white sometimes. She's our dog.
A: Is that her in the corner there? I can see an ear.
B: Yeah, that's her. She's a Staffie, she's old now, her hips are dodgy. She just sleeps on me.
A: Ah, bless her. We never had a dog, me mam wouldn't have it. My daughter's always on about one, Ellie, she's nine. Every other weekend she asks.
B: Aww. Is that her in the photo behind you?
A: Aye, that's her school photo. She hates it 'cause her fringe is wonky.
B: She looks lovely.
A: Ta. She's a good kid. Er, yeah. What do you get up to when you're not at work, then?
B: Erm, not much really. Walk Dolly. Jigsaws in winter, I've had one on the go three weeks. And a quiz down the pub with my sister.
A: Are you any good?
B: Not really, my sister is. I do the music round. Nineties stuff, do you know what I mean.
A: You'd be alright with me then, I only know Oasis.
B: *(laughs)* That's half the round, to be fair.
A: Ha, aye. Here, what's the food like at a depot? Do they feed yous?
B: There's a bacon bap van outside. Best bit of the job, honestly.
A: A bap. Me mam calls 'em bread buns. She'd have a fit if I said bap in the house—
